entities.name: Great Barrier Reef
entities.fact: The Great Barrier Reef stretches more than 2,300 kilometres along Australia's north-east coast and is the largest structure ever built by living things.

entities.name: Belize Barrier Reef
entities.fact: The Belize Barrier Reef runs about 300 kilometres along the coast of Belize and is the largest section of the Mesoamerican Reef.

entities.name: Mesoamerican Reef
entities.fact: The Mesoamerican Reef runs about 1,000 kilometres from Mexico's Yucatán to Honduras and is the largest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere.

entities.name: Florida Reef
entities.fact: The Florida Reef is the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States, running from near Miami to the Dry Tortugas.

entities.name: Ningaloo Reef
entities.fact: Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia is a fringing reef that hugs the shore so closely you can swim to it from the beach, and whale sharks gather there each year.

entities.name: Tubbataha Reef
entities.fact: The Tubbataha Reefs in the Philippines' Sulu Sea are two coral atolls so rich in life that they were made a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

entities.name: Bikini Atoll
entities.fact: Bikini Atoll's reef was blasted by 23 nuclear tests between 1946 and 1958, yet its corals have since grown back vigorously.

entities.name: Raja Ampat
entities.fact: The reefs of Raja Ampat in Indonesia hold more coral and reef-fish species than almost anywhere else on Earth, at the heart of the Coral Triangle.

entities.name: New Caledonia Barrier Reef
entities.fact: The New Caledonia Barrier Reef is the second-longest double barrier reef in the world and encloses one of the largest lagoons on Earth.

entities.name: Andros Barrier Reef
entities.fact: The Andros Barrier Reef in the Bahamas runs about 190 kilometres and drops away into the Tongue of the Ocean, a deep ocean trench.

entities.name: Apo Reef
entities.fact: Apo Reef off Mindoro in the Philippines is the largest atoll-like reef in the country and the second-largest contiguous coral reef in the world.

entities.name: Lighthouse Reef
entities.fact: Lighthouse Reef is an atoll off Belize whose lagoon contains the Great Blue Hole, a sinkhole about 125 metres deep made famous by Jacques Cousteau.

entities.name: Palancar Reef
entities.fact: Palancar Reef off Cozumel, Mexico, is part of the Mesoamerican Reef and became a famous dive site after Jacques Cousteau filmed it in the 1960s.

entities.name: Aldabra Atoll
entities.fact: Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles is one of the largest raised coral atolls in the world and home to about 100,000 giant tortoises.

entities.name: Kingman Reef
entities.fact: Kingman Reef is a nearly submerged coral atoll in the central Pacific with almost no dry land, yet its reef is one of the most pristine on Earth.

entities.name: Flower Garden Banks
aliases: Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary
entities.fact: The Flower Garden Banks are coral reefs growing on top of salt domes in the Gulf of Mexico, about 160 kilometres off the Texas coast.

entities.name: Great Sea Reef
entities.fact: Fiji's Great Sea Reef, known locally as Cakaulevu, is the third-longest continuous barrier reef in the world.

entities.name: Great Chagos Bank
entities.fact: The Great Chagos Bank in the Indian Ocean is the largest atoll structure in the world and is almost entirely submerged.

entities.name: Glover's Reef
entities.fact: Glover's Reef is an atoll off Belize named after the pirate John Glover and is a marine reserve known for its sheer outer walls.

entities.name: Turneffe Atoll
entities.fact: Turneffe Atoll off Belize is a large coral atoll whose mangrove islands and seagrass lagoons shelter manatees, crocodiles and bonefish.

entities.name: Lord Howe Island reef
entities.fact: The reef around Lord Howe Island, between Australia and New Zealand, is the southernmost coral reef in the world.

entities.name: Molasses Reef
entities.fact: Molasses Reef off Key Largo, Florida, is one of the most visited reefs in the world, lying inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary.

entities.name: Palmyra Atoll
entities.fact: Palmyra Atoll, an uninhabited US territory south of Hawaii, has reefs so untouched that predators like sharks make up most of the fish biomass.

entities.name: Kwajalein Atoll
entities.fact: Kwajalein Atoll in the Marshall Islands encloses one of the largest lagoons in the world, about 2,000 square kilometres.

entities.name: Rangiroa
entities.fact: Rangiroa in French Polynesia is one of the largest atolls in the world, with a lagoon so big that the whole island of Tahiti would fit inside it.

entities.name: Rowley Shoals
entities.fact: The Rowley Shoals are three atolls off north-west Australia that rise steeply from deep water and are famous for strong tidal currents and clear water.

entities.name: Scott Reef
entities.fact: Scott Reef is a remote atoll system off north-west Australia that recovered remarkably after being devastated by coral bleaching in 1998.

entities.name: Enewetak Atoll
entities.fact: Enewetak Atoll in the Marshall Islands was the site of 43 nuclear tests, and deep drilling into its reef in 1952 proved Darwin's theory of how atolls form.

entities.name: Abrolhos Bank
entities.fact: The Abrolhos Bank off Brazil holds the largest coral reefs in the South Atlantic, built into mushroom-shaped pillars found nowhere else.

entities.name: Osprey Reef
entities.fact: Osprey Reef is a submerged atoll in the Coral Sea off Queensland whose walls plunge about 1,000 metres and attract shark-diving expeditions.

entities.name: Ribbon Reefs
entities.fact: The Ribbon Reefs are a chain of ten long, narrow reefs on the outer Great Barrier Reef, home to the famous Cod Hole dive site.

entities.name: Sanganeb Atoll
entities.fact: Sanganeb is the only atoll in the Red Sea, rising off the coast of Sudan and protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

entities.name: Minerva Reefs
entities.fact: The Minerva Reefs are two remote atolls south of Fiji, claimed by Tonga, that briefly hosted a self-declared micronation in 1972.

entities.name: Amazon Reef
entities.fact: The Amazon Reef was only fully described in 2016, a reef system hidden under the muddy plume of the Amazon River where few thought reefs could grow.

entities.name: Mariana Trench
entities.fact: The Mariana Trench holds the Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the ocean at about 10,935 metres.

entities.name: Puerto Rico Trench
entities.fact: The Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest point in the Atlantic Ocean, reaching about 8,400 metres at the Milwaukee Deep.

entities.name: Japan Trench
entities.fact: The Japan Trench runs off north-east Honshu, and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake that caused the Fukushima disaster ruptured along it.

entities.name: Philippine Trench
entities.fact: The Philippine Trench off Mindanao reaches about 10,500 metres at the Emden Deep, named after the German cruiser that sounded it in 1927.

entities.name: Tonga Trench
entities.fact: The Tonga Trench is the second-deepest trench on Earth, reaching about 10,800 metres at the Horizon Deep.

entities.name: Java Trench
entities.fact: The Java Trench, also called the Sunda Trench, is the deepest point in the Indian Ocean at more than 7,000 metres, and the 2004 tsunami began along it.

entities.name: Kermadec Trench
entities.fact: The Kermadec Trench north-east of New Zealand plunges to about 10,000 metres and is home to huge swarms of amphipods and snailfish.

entities.name: Peru-Chile Trench
entities.fact: The Peru-Chile Trench, or Atacama Trench, runs about 5,900 kilometres along South America's Pacific coast and reaches about 8,000 metres deep.

entities.name: Aleutian Trench
entities.fact: The Aleutian Trench curves for about 3,400 kilometres south of Alaska's Aleutian Islands and reaches more than 7,600 metres deep.

entities.name: Kuril-Kamchatka Trench
entities.fact: The Kuril-Kamchatka Trench runs south from Kamchatka past the Kuril Islands and reaches more than 9,000 metres deep.

entities.name: South Sandwich Trench
entities.fact: The South Sandwich Trench east of the South Sandwich Islands is the deepest trench in the South Atlantic, reaching about 8,300 metres at the Meteor Deep.

entities.name: Izu-Ogasawara Trench
entities.fact: The Izu-Ogasawara Trench runs south from Japan to join the Mariana Trench and reaches more than 9,700 metres deep.

entities.name: Cayman Trough
entities.fact: The Cayman Trough is the deepest part of the Caribbean Sea, at about 7,500 metres, and holds the deepest known hydrothermal vents, the Beebe vent field.

entities.name: Ryukyu Trench
entities.fact: The Ryukyu Trench runs along the Ryukyu Islands between Japan and Taiwan and reaches about 7,500 metres deep.

entities.name: Middle America Trench
entities.fact: The Middle America Trench runs along the Pacific coast of Central America from Mexico to Costa Rica and reaches about 6,600 metres deep.

entities.name: Hikurangi Trench
entities.fact: The Hikurangi Trench off the east coast of New Zealand's North Island is where the Pacific Plate dives beneath the Australian Plate.

entities.name: Yap Trench
entities.fact: The Yap Trench lies south-west of the Mariana Trench near the island of Yap and reaches about 8,500 metres deep.

entities.name: Palau Trench
entities.fact: The Palau Trench lies east of the islands of Palau in the western Pacific and reaches about 8,000 metres deep.

entities.name: New Britain Trench
entities.fact: The New Britain Trench off Papua New Guinea drops to about 9,000 metres and has been explored by robotic landers dropped from the surface.

entities.name: Bougainville Trench
entities.fact: The Bougainville Trench lies south of Bougainville Island in the Solomon Sea and reaches more than 9,000 metres deep.

entities.name: San Cristobal Trench
entities.fact: The San Cristobal Trench runs south of the Solomon Islands and is part of the chain of trenches along the Pacific's Ring of Fire.

entities.name: Manila Trench
entities.fact: The Manila Trench lies west of Luzon in the South China Sea and reaches about 5,400 metres deep.

entities.name: New Hebrides Trench
entities.fact: The New Hebrides Trench near Vanuatu reaches about 7,600 metres, and a 2013 expedition found it full of cusk eels and prawns rather than the snailfish seen in other trenches.

entities.name: Puysegur Trench
entities.fact: The Puysegur Trench off the south-west tip of New Zealand is where the Australian Plate begins to slide beneath the Pacific Plate.

entities.name: South Shetland Trench
entities.fact: The South Shetland Trench north of the Antarctic Peninsula is one of the few ocean trenches in Antarctic waters.

entities.name: Makran Trench
entities.fact: The Makran Trench in the Arabian Sea, off Pakistan and Iran, is a shallow trench where the Arabian Plate slides beneath Eurasia.

entities.name: Hjort Trench
entities.fact: The Hjort Trench south of New Zealand and Macquarie Island is one of the southernmost trenches in the world, reaching about 6,700 metres.

entities.name: Vityaz Trench
entities.fact: The Vityaz Trench north of Fiji is named after the Soviet research ship Vityaz, which surveyed the Pacific's deepest trenches in the 1950s.

entities.name: Mussau Trench
entities.fact: The Mussau Trench north of Papua New Guinea is a young, short trench reaching about 7,000 metres deep.

entities.name: Nankai Trough
entities.fact: The Nankai Trough off southern Japan is a subduction trench feared for the huge earthquakes it produces roughly every 100 to 150 years.

entities.name: Hellenic Trench
entities.fact: The Hellenic Trench, curving south of Greece and Crete, contains the Calypso Deep, the deepest point in the Mediterranean at about 5,100 metres.

entities.name: Caribbean Sea
entities.fact: The Caribbean Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic enclosed by the Antilles and Central America, and its Cayman Trough is more than 7,000 metres deep.

entities.name: Gulf of Mexico
entities.fact: The Gulf of Mexico is an ocean basin of the Atlantic almost encircled by Mexico, Cuba and the United States, and the Mississippi River drains into it.

entities.name: North Sea
entities.fact: The North Sea is a shallow arm of the Atlantic between Britain and mainland Europe, averaging only about 90 metres deep.

entities.name: Mediterranean Sea
entities.fact: The Mediterranean is almost landlocked, connected to the Atlantic only through the Strait of Gibraltar, and evaporates far more water than its rivers bring in.

entities.name: Baltic Sea
entities.fact: The Baltic Sea is a brackish arm of the Atlantic so diluted by rivers that parts of it freeze over every winter.

entities.name: Sargasso Sea
entities.fact: The Sargasso Sea is the only sea with no coastline, bounded instead by Atlantic currents, and both European and American eels spawn there.

entities.name: Bay of Fundy
entities.fact: The Bay of Fundy between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick has the highest tides in the world, rising and falling by as much as 16 metres.

entities.name: Bay of Biscay
entities.fact: The Bay of Biscay, between France and Spain, is notorious among sailors for its violent Atlantic storms.

entities.name: Irish Sea
entities.fact: The Irish Sea separates Ireland from Great Britain and opens to the Atlantic through the North Channel and St George's Channel.

entities.name: Gulf of Guinea
entities.fact: The Gulf of Guinea is the great bend of the African coast where the equator and the prime meridian cross in open water.

entities.name: Labrador Sea
entities.fact: The Labrador Sea between Canada and Greenland is one of the few places where surface water sinks to the deep ocean, helping drive global circulation.

entities.name: Celtic Sea
entities.fact: The Celtic Sea lies south of Ireland and west of Cornwall and was only given its name in 1921.

entities.name: Gulf of St Lawrence
entities.fact: The Gulf of St Lawrence is the largest estuary in the world, where the St Lawrence River meets the Atlantic, and it freezes over in winter.

entities.name: Chesapeake Bay
entities.fact: Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States and is famous for its blue crabs and oysters.

entities.name: Gulf of Maine
entities.fact: The Gulf of Maine is one of the fastest-warming bodies of water in the world and borders the famous Georges Bank fishing grounds.

entities.name: Delaware Bay
entities.fact: Delaware Bay hosts the world's largest spawning gathering of horseshoe crabs each spring, feeding millions of migrating shorebirds.

entities.name: Gulf of Bothnia
entities.fact: The Gulf of Bothnia, the northern arm of the Baltic, is so fresh and cold that it is largely frozen for months each winter.

entities.name: Gulf of Cádiz
entities.fact: The Gulf of Cádiz lies off south-west Spain and Portugal just outside the Strait of Gibraltar, where salty Mediterranean water pours out into the Atlantic.

entities.name: Gulf of Finland
entities.fact: The Gulf of Finland is the easternmost arm of the Baltic Sea, with St Petersburg at its head and Helsinki and Tallinn on its shores.

entities.name: Wadden Sea
entities.fact: The Wadden Sea is a shallow, tidal stretch of the North Sea with the world's largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats.

entities.name: Bay of Campeche
entities.fact: The Bay of Campeche is the southern bight of the Gulf of Mexico, site of the huge Cantarell oil field and part of the Chicxulub impact crater.

entities.name: Gulf of Venezuela
entities.fact: The Gulf of Venezuela opens off the Caribbean and connects through a narrow channel to Lake Maracaibo, one of the world's oldest oil regions.

entities.name: Gulf of Honduras
entities.fact: The Gulf of Honduras is a Caribbean inlet bordered by Belize, Guatemala and Honduras at the southern end of the Mesoamerican Reef.

entities.name: Bight of Benin
entities.fact: The Bight of Benin is a bay in the Gulf of Guinea whose shore was once known as the Slave Coast.

entities.name: Gulf of Paria
entities.fact: The Gulf of Paria is a shallow inlet between Trinidad and Venezuela, fed by the muddy waters of the Orinoco delta.

entities.name: Cardigan Bay
entities.fact: Cardigan Bay is the largest bay in Wales and home to a resident population of bottlenose dolphins.

entities.name: Gulf of Riga
entities.fact: The Gulf of Riga is a bay of the Baltic Sea enclosed by Latvia and Estonia and nearly cut off from the open sea by the island of Saaremaa.

entities.name: Bight of Biafra
entities.fact: The Bight of Biafra, now officially the Bight of Bonny, is the easternmost corner of the Gulf of Guinea, off Nigeria and Cameroon.

entities.name: Gulf of San Jorge
entities.fact: The Gulf of San Jorge is a wide bay on the Patagonian coast of Argentina, open to the South Atlantic.

entities.name: Walvis Bay
entities.fact: Walvis Bay on the coast of Namibia is a natural deep-water harbour whose name means whale bay in Afrikaans.

entities.name: Guanabara Bay
entities.fact: Guanabara Bay is the great bay on which Rio de Janeiro stands, named by Portuguese sailors who mistook it for a river mouth in January 1502.

entities.name: Bay of All Saints
entities.fact: The Bay of All Saints at Salvador is the largest bay in Brazil and was named by Portuguese explorers who arrived on All Saints' Day in 1501.

entities.name: Bay of Pigs
entities.fact: The Bay of Pigs is an inlet on Cuba's southern Caribbean coast, famous for the failed 1961 invasion by CIA-trained Cuban exiles.

entities.name: South China Sea
entities.fact: The South China Sea is a marginal sea of the western Pacific crossed by roughly a third of the world's shipping.

entities.name: Sea of Japan
entities.fact: The Sea of Japan, called the East Sea in Korea, is a marginal sea of the Pacific nearly enclosed by Japan, Korea and Russia.

entities.name: Bering Sea
entities.fact: The Bering Sea separates Alaska from Siberia and is named after Vitus Bering, the Danish navigator who sailed through it for Russia in 1728.

entities.name: Gulf of California
entities.fact: The Gulf of California, also called the Sea of Cortez after the conquistador Hernán Cortés, separates Baja California from mainland Mexico and is home to the vaquita.

entities.name: Coral Sea
entities.fact: The Coral Sea off north-east Australia contains the Great Barrier Reef, and a 1942 battle fought there was the first in which opposing ships never sighted each other.

entities.name: Tasman Sea
entities.fact: The Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand is named after the Dutch explorer Abel Tasman, who sailed it in 1642, and is nicknamed the Ditch.

entities.name: East China Sea
entities.fact: The East China Sea lies between China and Japan's Ryukyu Islands and receives the muddy outflow of the Yangtze River.

entities.name: Gulf of Alaska
entities.fact: The Gulf of Alaska is a wide arm of the Pacific along Alaska's southern coast where glaciers meet the sea and ferocious winter storms are born.

entities.name: Philippine Sea
entities.fact: The Philippine Sea, east of the Philippines, is the largest sea in the world by area and contains the Mariana Trench.

entities.name: Sea of Okhotsk
entities.fact: The Sea of Okhotsk, off Russia's far east, is the coldest sea in East Asia and is covered by drifting ice for much of the winter.

entities.name: Yellow Sea
entities.fact: The Yellow Sea between China and Korea takes its name from the yellow silt carried into it by the Yellow River.

entities.name: Gulf of Thailand
entities.fact: The Gulf of Thailand is a shallow inlet of the South China Sea, bordered by Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

entities.name: Celebes Sea
entities.fact: The Celebes Sea between Indonesia and the Philippines is a deep basin of more than 6,000 metres, famous for the rich reefs around Sipadan.

entities.name: Sulu Sea
entities.fact: The Sulu Sea in the south-west Philippines holds the Tubbataha Reefs and is enclosed by Palawan, Borneo and the Sulu Archipelago.

entities.name: San Francisco Bay
entities.fact: San Francisco Bay is the largest estuary on the Pacific coast of the Americas, entered through the Golden Gate strait.

entities.name: Monterey Bay
entities.fact: Monterey Bay in California lies above a submarine canyon as deep as the Grand Canyon and is a sanctuary for sea otters and whales.

entities.name: Tokyo Bay
entities.fact: Tokyo Bay, the harbour of Tokyo and Yokohama, is where Commodore Perry's black ships arrived in 1853 to open Japan to trade.

entities.name: Banda Sea
entities.fact: The Banda Sea in eastern Indonesia is a deep basin surrounding the Banda Islands, the original source of nutmeg and mace.

entities.name: Bismarck Sea
entities.fact: The Bismarck Sea lies north-east of New Guinea and is named, like the Bismarck Archipelago, after the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

entities.name: Solomon Sea
entities.fact: The Solomon Sea lies between the Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea and was the scene of fierce naval battles in the Second World War.

entities.name: Gulf of Tonkin
entities.fact: The Gulf of Tonkin, between northern Vietnam and China, holds Halong Bay and gave its name to the 1964 incident that drew the United States deeper into the Vietnam War.

entities.name: Gulf of Panama
entities.fact: The Gulf of Panama is the Pacific entrance to the Panama Canal and has some of the largest tides in the tropics, unlike the tiny tides on the Caribbean side.

entities.name: Bohai Sea
entities.fact: The Bohai Sea is the innermost gulf of the Yellow Sea, almost enclosed by China's coast, and the sea approach to the port of Tianjin.

entities.name: Seto Inland Sea
entities.fact: The Seto Inland Sea separates three of Japan's main islands, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, and is dotted with about 3,000 islands.

entities.name: Puget Sound
entities.fact: Puget Sound is a deep, glacier-carved inlet of the Pacific in Washington state, named by George Vancouver after his lieutenant Peter Puget, with Seattle on its shore.

entities.name: Botany Bay
entities.fact: Botany Bay south of Sydney is where Captain Cook first landed in Australia in 1770, named for the plants collected there by Joseph Banks.

entities.name: Molucca Sea
entities.fact: The Molucca Sea lies between Sulawesi and the Maluku Islands, the Spice Islands that drew European traders to Indonesia.

entities.name: Leyte Gulf
entities.fact: Leyte Gulf in the Philippines saw the largest naval battle of the Second World War in October 1944.

entities.name: Gulf of Tehuantepec
entities.fact: The Gulf of Tehuantepec off southern Mexico is famous for violent gap winds that blast through the mountains and far out to sea.

entities.name: Bay of Plenty
entities.fact: The Bay of Plenty on New Zealand's North Island was named by Captain Cook in 1769 for the friendly welcome and abundant supplies he found there.

entities.name: Cenderawasih Bay
entities.fact: Cenderawasih Bay in Indonesian New Guinea is famous for whale sharks that gather beneath fishing platforms to feed on baitfish.

entities.name: Hangzhou Bay
entities.fact: Hangzhou Bay in eastern China produces the world's largest tidal bore, a wall of water that surges up the Qiantang River.

entities.name: Halong Bay
entities.fact: Halong Bay in northern Vietnam is studded with about 1,600 limestone islands and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

entities.name: Salish Sea
entities.fact: The Salish Sea, which includes Puget Sound and the Strait of Georgia, was only officially named in 2009, after the Coast Salish peoples.

entities.name: Strait of Gibraltar
entities.fact: The Strait of Gibraltar joins the Atlantic to the Mediterranean and is only about 14 kilometres wide at its narrowest, between Spain and Morocco.

entities.name: English Channel
entities.fact: The English Channel separates England from France and joins the Atlantic to the North Sea; it is about 34 kilometres across at the Strait of Dover.

entities.name: Bering Strait
entities.fact: The Bering Strait, named after the Danish navigator Vitus Bering, separates Russia from Alaska by about 82 kilometres and links the Pacific to the Arctic.

entities.name: Strait of Hormuz
entities.fact: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, and about a fifth of the world's oil passes through it.

entities.name: Bosporus
entities.fact: The Bosporus runs through the middle of Istanbul, linking the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and dividing Europe from Asia.

entities.name: Strait of Magellan
entities.fact: The Strait of Magellan, named after Ferdinand Magellan who sailed through it in 1520, lets ships pass between the Atlantic and Pacific south of mainland South America.

entities.name: Strait of Malacca
entities.fact: The Strait of Malacca between Malaysia and Sumatra is one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world, linking the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.

entities.name: Drake Passage
entities.fact: The Drake Passage between Cape Horn and Antarctica, named after Sir Francis Drake, has some of the roughest seas on Earth.

entities.name: Dardanelles
entities.fact: The Dardanelles, known in ancient times as the Hellespont, link the Sea of Marmara to the Aegean and were the scene of the Gallipoli campaign in 1915.

entities.name: Strait of Dover
entities.fact: The Strait of Dover is the narrowest part of the English Channel, about 33 kilometres wide, and one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

entities.name: Bass Strait
entities.fact: Bass Strait separates Tasmania from mainland Australia and is named after George Bass, the ship's surgeon who proved Tasmania was an island in 1798.

entities.name: Cook Strait
entities.fact: Cook Strait separates New Zealand's North and South Islands and is named after Captain James Cook, who sailed through it in 1770.

entities.name: Torres Strait
entities.fact: Torres Strait between Australia and New Guinea is named after the Spanish navigator Luis Váez de Torres, who sailed through it in 1606.

entities.name: Strait of Messina
entities.fact: The Strait of Messina between Sicily and mainland Italy is home to the whirlpools behind the legend of Scylla and Charybdis.

entities.name: Bab-el-Mandeb
entities.fact: The Bab-el-Mandeb, whose name means Gate of Tears, joins the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden between Yemen and Djibouti.

entities.name: Strait of Juan de Fuca
entities.fact: The Strait of Juan de Fuca between Washington state and Vancouver Island is named after a Greek sailor, known by his Spanish name Juan de Fuca, who claimed to have found it in 1592.

entities.name: Taiwan Strait
entities.fact: The Taiwan Strait separates Taiwan from mainland China and is about 130 kilometres wide at its narrowest.

entities.name: Davis Strait
entities.fact: Davis Strait between Baffin Island and Greenland is named after the English explorer John Davis, who sailed through it in the 1580s seeking the Northwest Passage.

entities.name: Denmark Strait
entities.fact: The Denmark Strait between Greenland and Iceland is where the Bismarck sank HMS Hood in 1941, and it carries the world's biggest underwater waterfall.

entities.name: Hudson Strait
entities.fact: Hudson Strait links Hudson Bay to the Labrador Sea and the Atlantic and is named after the English explorer Henry Hudson.

entities.name: Oresund
entities.fact: The Oresund between Denmark and Sweden is one of the three Danish straits linking the Baltic to the North Sea, now spanned by the Oresund Bridge.

entities.name: Skagerrak
entities.fact: The Skagerrak is the strait between Norway, Denmark and Sweden that links the North Sea to the Baltic, and it was the scene of the Battle of Jutland in 1916.

entities.name: Korea Strait
entities.fact: The Korea Strait between South Korea and Japan links the East China Sea to the Sea of Japan, and the Russian fleet was destroyed there at Tsushima in 1905.

entities.name: Sunda Strait
entities.fact: The Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra links the Java Sea to the Indian Ocean and holds the volcano Krakatoa.

entities.name: Mozambique Channel
entities.fact: The Mozambique Channel separates Madagascar from the African mainland, and the coelacanth was found alive in the Comoros at its northern end.

entities.name: Yucatán Channel
entities.fact: The Yucatán Channel between Mexico and Cuba links the Caribbean Sea to the Gulf of Mexico and carries the current that becomes the Gulf Stream.

entities.name: Strait of Bonifacio
entities.fact: The Strait of Bonifacio separates Corsica from Sardinia and is notorious for strong winds and shipwrecks.

entities.name: Strait of Otranto
entities.fact: The Strait of Otranto between Italy and Albania is the gateway from the Ionian Sea into the Adriatic.

entities.name: Windward Passage
entities.fact: The Windward Passage between Cuba and Haiti connects the Atlantic to the Caribbean and is the main shipping route from the US east coast to the Panama Canal.

entities.name: Lombok Strait
entities.fact: The Lombok Strait between Bali and Lombok marks part of the Wallace Line, the boundary between Asian and Australian wildlife.

entities.name: Palk Strait
entities.fact: Palk Strait between India and Sri Lanka is so shallow that large ships cannot pass, and a chain of shoals called Adam's Bridge lies at its southern end.

entities.name: Pentland Firth
entities.fact: The Pentland Firth between mainland Scotland and Orkney has some of the fastest tidal currents in the world, used today to generate electricity.

entities.name: Tsugaru Strait
entities.fact: The Tsugaru Strait separates Honshu from Hokkaido and is crossed by the Seikan Tunnel, one of the longest rail tunnels in the world.

entities.name: Cabot Strait
entities.fact: Cabot Strait between Newfoundland and Cape Breton Island is named after the explorer John Cabot and is the main entrance to the Gulf of St Lawrence.

entities.name: Golden Gate
entities.fact: The Golden Gate is the strait connecting San Francisco Bay to the Pacific, and its famous bridge was for decades the longest suspension bridge in the world.

entities.name: Hudson Bay
entities.fact: Hudson Bay is a vast inland sea in Canada named after the English explorer Henry Hudson, who was set adrift there by mutineers in 1611 and never seen again.

entities.name: Beaufort Sea
entities.fact: The Beaufort Sea north of Alaska and Canada is named after Sir Francis Beaufort, the British admiral who devised the Beaufort wind scale.

entities.name: Weddell Sea
entities.fact: The Weddell Sea off Antarctica is named after the British sealer James Weddell, who sailed into it in 1823, and its pack ice crushed Shackleton's ship Endurance in 1915.

entities.name: Ross Sea
entities.fact: The Ross Sea is a deep bay of Antarctica named after James Clark Ross, who discovered it in 1841, and it is fringed by the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest in the world.

entities.name: Amundsen Sea
entities.fact: The Amundsen Sea off West Antarctica is named after the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and is where the fast-melting Thwaites Glacier flows into the sea.

entities.name: Barents Sea
entities.fact: The Barents Sea north of Norway and Russia is named after the Dutch navigator Willem Barentsz, who died there in 1597 after wintering on Novaya Zemlya.

entities.name: Baffin Bay
entities.fact: Baffin Bay between Greenland and Baffin Island is named after William Baffin, the English navigator who explored it in 1616.

entities.name: Bellingshausen Sea
entities.fact: The Bellingshausen Sea off Antarctica is named after Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen, the Russian officer whose expedition sighted the continent in 1820.

entities.name: Laptev Sea
entities.fact: The Laptev Sea off Siberia is named after the Russian explorer cousins Dmitry and Khariton Laptev, who charted the Arctic coast in the 1730s and 1740s.

entities.name: Lincoln Sea
entities.fact: The Lincoln Sea, north of Greenland and Ellesmere Island, is named after Robert Todd Lincoln, US Secretary of War and son of Abraham Lincoln.

entities.name: James Bay
entities.fact: James Bay, the southern arm of Hudson Bay, is named after Thomas James, the Welsh captain who wintered on its shore in 1631.

entities.name: Frobisher Bay
entities.fact: Frobisher Bay on Baffin Island is named after Martin Frobisher, who sailed into it in 1576 searching for the Northwest Passage and brought home worthless ore he took for gold.

entities.name: Foxe Basin
entities.fact: Foxe Basin north of Hudson Bay is named after Luke Foxe, the English explorer who searched it for the Northwest Passage in 1631.

entities.name: Dampier Strait
entities.fact: Dampier Strait in Papua New Guinea is named after William Dampier, the English buccaneer and naturalist who sailed through it in 1700.

entities.name: Bransfield Strait
entities.fact: Bransfield Strait between the South Shetland Islands and the Antarctic Peninsula is named after Edward Bransfield, who charted the area in 1820.

entities.name: Gerlache Strait
entities.fact: The Gerlache Strait along the Antarctic Peninsula is named after Adrien de Gerlache, the Belgian whose expedition was the first to winter in the Antarctic, in 1898.

entities.name: Nares Strait
entities.fact: Nares Strait between Greenland and Ellesmere Island is named after George Nares, the British admiral who led an expedition towards the North Pole in 1875.

entities.name: Lancaster Sound
entities.fact: Lancaster Sound, the eastern entrance to the Northwest Passage, is named after Sir James Lancaster, a sponsor of William Baffin's 1616 voyage.

entities.name: Gulf of Carpentaria
entities.fact: The Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia is named after Pieter de Carpentier, a governor-general of the Dutch East Indies, and hosts the Morning Glory cloud.

entities.name: Joseph Bonaparte Gulf
entities.fact: The Joseph Bonaparte Gulf in northern Australia was named by the French explorer Nicolas Baudin after Napoleon's elder brother Joseph.

entities.name: Adriatic Sea
entities.fact: The Adriatic Sea separates Italy from the Balkans and is the arm of the Mediterranean on which Venice was built.

entities.name: Aegean Sea
entities.fact: The Aegean Sea between Greece and Turkey is scattered with hundreds of islands, and its ancient trade routes made it the cradle of Greek civilisation.

entities.name: Ionian Sea
entities.fact: The Ionian Sea lies between southern Italy and western Greece and holds the deepest point in the Mediterranean, the Calypso Deep at about 5,100 metres.

entities.name: Tyrrhenian Sea
entities.fact: The Tyrrhenian Sea, between Italy's west coast, Sardinia, Corsica and Sicily, is named after the Tyrrhenians, the Greek name for the Etruscans.

entities.name: Black Sea
entities.fact: The Black Sea connects to the Mediterranean only through the Bosporus and Dardanelles, and below about 150 metres its water contains no oxygen at all.

entities.name: Ligurian Sea
entities.fact: The Ligurian Sea, between the Italian Riviera and Corsica, is part of the Pelagos Sanctuary, a protected area rich in fin whales and dolphins.

entities.name: Balearic Sea
entities.fact: The Balearic Sea lies between the east coast of Spain and the Balearic Islands of Majorca, Minorca and Ibiza.

entities.name: Sea of Marmara
entities.fact: The Sea of Marmara is a small inland sea entirely within Turkey, linking the Black Sea to the Aegean through the Bosporus and Dardanelles.

entities.name: Alboran Sea
entities.fact: The Alboran Sea is the westernmost part of the Mediterranean, just inside the Strait of Gibraltar, where Atlantic water first flows in.

entities.name: Levantine Sea
entities.fact: The Levantine Sea is the easternmost part of the Mediterranean, off Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Egypt, and the saltiest part of the whole sea.

entities.name: Gulf of Lion
entities.fact: The Gulf of Lion on the south coast of France is swept by the mistral wind and receives the waters of the Rhône.

entities.name: Gulf of Genoa
entities.fact: The Gulf of Genoa is the northernmost part of the Ligurian Sea, with the port of Genoa, birthplace of Christopher Columbus, at its head.

entities.name: Gulf of Taranto
entities.fact: The Gulf of Taranto is the large bay in the instep of Italy's boot, opening onto the Ionian Sea.

entities.name: Gulf of Sidra
entities.fact: The Gulf of Sidra on the coast of Libya was claimed by Gaddafi as Libyan waters behind a Line of Death, leading to clashes with the US Navy in the 1980s.

entities.name: Sea of Crete
entities.fact: The Sea of Crete is the southern part of the Aegean between Crete and the Cyclades, and is deeper than most of the Aegean.

entities.name: Gulf of Corinth
entities.fact: The Gulf of Corinth nearly cuts the Peloponnese off from mainland Greece, and the Corinth Canal, finished in 1893, links it to the Saronic Gulf.

entities.name: Sea of Azov
entities.fact: The Sea of Azov, linked to the Black Sea by the Kerch Strait, is the shallowest sea in the world, averaging only about 7 metres deep.

entities.name: Gulf of Venice
entities.fact: The Gulf of Venice is the northern end of the Adriatic Sea, so shallow that Venice floods whenever strong winds push water into it.

entities.name: Libyan Sea
entities.fact: The Libyan Sea is the stretch of the Mediterranean between Crete and the coast of Libya.

entities.name: Thracian Sea
entities.fact: The Thracian Sea is the northernmost part of the Aegean, off the coasts of Greek Thrace and Macedonia and the island of Thasos.

entities.name: Myrtoan Sea
entities.fact: The Myrtoan Sea is the part of the Aegean between the Cyclades and the eastern coast of the Peloponnese.

entities.name: Icarian Sea
entities.fact: The Icarian Sea is the part of the Aegean around the island of Icaria, where in legend Icarus fell into the sea after flying too close to the sun.

entities.name: Gulf of Gabès
entities.fact: The Gulf of Gabès off Tunisia has the largest tides in the Mediterranean, up to about 2 metres, in a sea where tides are usually tiny.

entities.name: Gulf of Tunis
entities.fact: The Gulf of Tunis is a bay of the Mediterranean on which the ruins of ancient Carthage stand, near the modern city of Tunis.

entities.name: Gulf of Trieste
entities.fact: The Gulf of Trieste is the northernmost point of the Adriatic and of the whole Mediterranean, shared by Italy, Slovenia and Croatia.

entities.name: Saronic Gulf
entities.fact: The Saronic Gulf is the bay of the Aegean on which Athens and its port Piraeus stand, where the Greeks crushed the Persian fleet at Salamis in 480 BC.

entities.name: Gulf of Naples
entities.fact: The Gulf of Naples is overlooked by Mount Vesuvius, whose eruption in AD 79 buried Pompeii, and holds the islands of Capri and Ischia.

entities.name: Gulf of Antalya
entities.fact: The Gulf of Antalya on Turkey's southern coast is a wide bay of the Levantine Sea backed by the Taurus Mountains.

entities.name: Sea of Sardinia
entities.fact: The Sea of Sardinia is the stretch of the western Mediterranean between Sardinia and the Balearic Islands.

entities.name: Gulf of Hammamet
entities.fact: The Gulf of Hammamet is a bay on Tunisia's east coast lined with beach resorts.

entities.name: Gulf of Salerno
entities.fact: The Gulf of Salerno, south of the Amalfi Coast, was where Allied troops landed in Italy in September 1943.

entities.name: Gulf of İskenderun
entities.fact: The Gulf of İskenderun in the far north-east corner of the Mediterranean is where the Turkish coast turns south towards Syria, near the ancient battlefield of Issus.

entities.name: Thermaic Gulf
entities.fact: The Thermaic Gulf is the arm of the Aegean at whose head stands Thessaloniki, Greece's second city.

entities.name: Kvarner Gulf
entities.fact: The Kvarner Gulf is a bay of the northern Adriatic in Croatia, sheltered by the islands of Krk, Cres and Rab, with the port of Rijeka at its head.

entities.name: Pagasetic Gulf
entities.fact: The Pagasetic Gulf is an almost enclosed bay of the Aegean in Thessaly from whose shore, in legend, Jason and the Argonauts set sail for the Golden Fleece.

entities.name: Gulf Stream
entities.fact: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico up the US east coast and across the Atlantic, keeping north-west Europe far milder than its latitude suggests.

entities.name: Humboldt Current
entities.fact: The Humboldt Current carries cold, nutrient-rich water north along the coast of Chile and Peru, feeding the world's largest anchovy fishery.

entities.name: East Australian Current
entities.fact: The East Australian Current sweeps warm water south along Australia's east coast and was the EAC ridden by the turtles in Finding Nemo.

entities.name: California Current
entities.fact: The California Current flows south along the US west coast, bringing cold water and the fog for which San Francisco is famous.

entities.name: Kuroshio Current
entities.fact: The Kuroshio, or Black Stream, is the Pacific's counterpart to the Gulf Stream, carrying warm water north past Japan.

entities.name: North Atlantic Drift
entities.fact: The North Atlantic Drift is the continuation of the Gulf Stream that carries warm water towards Britain, Norway and the Arctic.

entities.name: Antarctic Circumpolar Current
entities.fact: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current circles the whole of Antarctica unbroken by land and is the largest ocean current on Earth, carrying more water than any other.

entities.name: Labrador Current
entities.fact: The Labrador Current carries cold Arctic water and icebergs south past Newfoundland, and it was one of its icebergs that sank the Titanic.

entities.name: Canary Current
entities.fact: The Canary Current flows south past north-west Africa and the Canary Islands and helped carry Columbus's ships towards the Caribbean.

entities.name: Benguela Current
entities.fact: The Benguela Current carries cold, nutrient-rich water north along the coast of Namibia and South Africa, supporting vast shoals of sardines and the Namib coast's fogs.

entities.name: Agulhas Current
entities.fact: The Agulhas Current races south along the east coast of South Africa and, meeting opposing winds, produces some of the world's most dangerous rogue waves.

entities.name: Brazil Current
entities.fact: The Brazil Current carries warm tropical water south along the coast of Brazil until it meets the cold Falkland Current off Argentina.

entities.name: North Equatorial Current
entities.fact: The North Equatorial Current flows westward just north of the equator in both the Atlantic and the Pacific, driven by the trade winds.

entities.name: Equatorial Counter Current
entities.fact: The Equatorial Counter Current flows eastward against the trade winds in a narrow band near the equator, between the westward-flowing equatorial currents.

entities.name: Oyashio Current
entities.fact: The Oyashio is a cold current flowing south from the Bering Sea past Kamchatka, and where it meets the warm Kuroshio it creates rich fishing grounds off Japan.

entities.name: Florida Current
entities.fact: The Florida Current squeezes between Florida and the Bahamas as the start of the Gulf Stream and carries far more water than all the world's rivers combined.

entities.name: Alaska Current
entities.fact: The Alaska Current carries relatively warm water anticlockwise around the Gulf of Alaska, keeping the coast of the Alaska panhandle milder and wetter.

entities.name: Loop Current
entities.fact: The Loop Current curls up into the Gulf of Mexico and back out past Florida, and its deep warm water can strengthen hurricanes passing over it.

entities.name: Falkland Current
entities.fact: The Falkland Current carries cold Antarctic water north along the coast of Argentina, bringing Magellanic penguins as far north as Brazil.

entities.name: Leeuwin Current
entities.fact: The Leeuwin Current flows south along the coast of Western Australia, carrying warm tropical water that lets corals grow as far south as the Abrolhos Islands.

entities.name: North Pacific Gyre
entities.fact: The North Pacific Gyre is the huge clockwise circulation of the North Pacific whose calm centre collects floating plastic in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

entities.name: North Atlantic Gyre
entities.fact: The North Atlantic Gyre is the clockwise loop formed by the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Canary Current and North Equatorial Current, enclosing the Sargasso Sea.

entities.name: East Greenland Current
entities.fact: The East Greenland Current carries cold water and sea ice south from the Arctic along Greenland's east coast and through the Denmark Strait.

entities.name: South Equatorial Current
entities.fact: The South Equatorial Current flows westward along the equator, and in the Atlantic it splits on the coast of Brazil to feed both the Brazil Current and the Guiana Current.

entities.name: Guinea Current
entities.fact: The Guinea Current flows eastward along the coast of West Africa into the Gulf of Guinea.

entities.name: Irminger Current
entities.fact: The Irminger Current is a warm branch of the North Atlantic Drift that flows west past Iceland towards Greenland.

entities.name: Somali Current
entities.fact: The Somali Current off the Horn of Africa is one of the few currents that reverses direction, flowing north in the summer monsoon and south in winter.

entities.name: Norwegian Current
entities.fact: The Norwegian Current carries warm Atlantic water north along the coast of Norway, keeping its harbours ice-free even beyond the Arctic Circle.

entities.name: Beaufort Gyre
entities.fact: The Beaufort Gyre is a wind-driven clockwise circulation in the Arctic Ocean north of Alaska that stores a huge volume of fresh water from melting ice.

entities.name: Antilles Current
entities.fact: The Antilles Current flows north-west along the outer edge of the Caribbean islands and joins the Florida Current to form the Gulf Stream.

entities.name: Transpolar Drift
entities.fact: The Transpolar Drift carries sea ice from Siberia across the North Pole towards Greenland, and it carried Nansen's ship Fram across the Arctic.

entities.name: West Australian Current
entities.fact: The West Australian Current is the cold northward flow on the eastern side of the Indian Ocean gyre, offshore of the warm Leeuwin Current.

entities.name: Cromwell Current
entities.fact: The Cromwell Current is a hidden river of water flowing east beneath the surface of the equatorial Pacific, discovered only in 1952.

entities.name: Hawaii
entities.fact: The Hawaiian Islands are the tops of volcanoes built over a hotspot, and Mauna Kea is the tallest mountain on Earth measured from its base on the sea floor.

entities.name: Fiji
entities.fact: Fiji is a nation of more than 300 islands in the South Pacific, and its Great Sea Reef is one of the longest barrier reefs in the world.

entities.name: Tahiti
entities.fact: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia, a volcanic peak ringed by reef, where Captain Cook observed the transit of Venus in 1769.

entities.name: Galápagos Islands
entities.fact: The Galápagos Islands straddle the equator about 1,000 kilometres off Ecuador, and their finches and tortoises helped inspire Darwin's theory of evolution.

entities.name: New Zealand
entities.fact: New Zealand's two main islands sit alone in the South Pacific, and their isolation produced flightless birds like the kiwi and the extinct giant moa.

entities.name: Easter Island
entities.fact: Easter Island is one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth, more than 3,500 kilometres from Chile, and is famous for its giant stone moai.

entities.name: Bora Bora
entities.fact: Bora Bora is a volcanic island in French Polynesia surrounded by a turquoise lagoon and a ring of reef islets.

entities.name: Japan
entities.fact: Japan is an archipelago of thousands of islands in the western Pacific, dominated by the four large islands of Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku.

entities.name: Guam
entities.fact: Guam is the largest of the Mariana Islands and lies close to the Mariana Trench, the deepest part of the ocean.

entities.name: Samoa
entities.fact: The Samoan Islands in the central Pacific are divided between the independent nation of Samoa and the US territory of American Samoa.

entities.name: Tonga
entities.fact: Tonga is a kingdom of about 170 islands in the South Pacific, and the Tonga Trench off its coast is the second-deepest in the world.

entities.name: Philippines
entities.fact: The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands between the South China Sea and the Pacific.

entities.name: Solomon Islands
entities.fact: The Solomon Islands in the south-west Pacific include Guadalcanal, where a brutal six-month battle was fought in 1942 and 1943.

entities.name: Vanuatu
entities.fact: Vanuatu is a chain of about 80 volcanic islands in the South Pacific, including Tanna with its easily visited active volcano, Mount Yasur.

entities.name: New Caledonia
entities.fact: New Caledonia is a French territory in the south-west Pacific whose main island is ringed by one of the longest barrier reefs in the world.

entities.name: Marshall Islands
entities.fact: The Marshall Islands are 29 low coral atolls in the central Pacific, including Bikini and Enewetak, where the United States tested nuclear weapons.

entities.name: Okinawa
entities.fact: Okinawa is the largest of Japan's Ryukyu Islands, in the East China Sea, and was the site of the last great battle of the Second World War in 1945.

entities.name: Iwo Jima
entities.fact: Iwo Jima is a small volcanic island south of Japan where US Marines raised the flag on Mount Suribachi in 1945.

entities.name: Midway Atoll
entities.fact: Midway Atoll lies near the end of the Hawaiian chain and gave its name to the 1942 battle that turned the Pacific War.

entities.name: Pitcairn Islands
entities.fact: Pitcairn Island was settled in 1790 by the mutineers of HMS Bounty and remains one of the least populated territories on Earth.

entities.name: Marquesas Islands
entities.fact: The Marquesas are rugged volcanic islands in French Polynesia without protecting reefs, where the painter Paul Gauguin spent his last years.

entities.name: Palau
entities.fact: Palau in the western Pacific is famous for its Rock Islands and for Jellyfish Lake, where millions of harmless jellyfish drift in a marine lake.

entities.name: Kiribati
entities.fact: Kiribati is spread across 33 islands straddling the equator and the International Date Line, and includes Kiritimati, the largest coral atoll by land area.

entities.name: Tuvalu
entities.fact: Tuvalu is a nation of nine low coral atolls in the Pacific whose highest point is only a few metres above sea level.

entities.name: Cook Islands
entities.fact: The Cook Islands are 15 islands in the South Pacific named after Captain James Cook and self-governing in free association with New Zealand.

entities.name: New Guinea
entities.fact: New Guinea is the second-largest island in the world and is home to the birds of paradise and more than 800 languages.

entities.name: Vancouver Island
entities.fact: Vancouver Island off Canada's west coast is the largest island on the Pacific coast of the Americas.

entities.name: Aleutian Islands
entities.fact: The Aleutian Islands are a chain of volcanic islands stretching about 1,900 kilometres west from Alaska towards Russia.

entities.name: Nauru
entities.fact: Nauru is a single raised coral island in the Pacific, the smallest island nation in the world, once rich from mining phosphate formed from seabird droppings.

entities.name: Tuamotu Islands
entities.fact: The Tuamotus are the largest chain of coral atolls in the world, about 80 low islands strung across French Polynesia.

entities.name: Chatham Islands
entities.fact: The Chatham Islands east of New Zealand are among the first inhabited places on Earth to see each new day.

entities.name: Kuril Islands
entities.fact: The Kuril Islands are a volcanic chain between Kamchatka and Japan, still disputed between Russia and Japan since the end of the Second World War.

entities.name: Farallon Islands
entities.fact: The Farallon Islands off San Francisco are a wildlife refuge where great white sharks gather each autumn to hunt seals.

entities.name: Clipperton Island
entities.fact: Clipperton Island is a tiny uninhabited French atoll in the eastern Pacific, more than 1,000 kilometres from Mexico, ringed by a lagoon and overrun by land crabs.

entities.name: Juan Fernández Islands
entities.fact: The Juan Fernández Islands off Chile include Robinson Crusoe Island, where the marooned sailor Alexander Selkirk survived alone for four years and inspired Defoe's novel.

entities.name: Iceland
entities.fact: Iceland sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, which is why it is so volcanic.

entities.name: Bermuda
entities.fact: Bermuda is a lone group of islands in the North Atlantic about 1,000 kilometres from the US coast, with the most northerly coral reefs in the world.

entities.name: Bahamas
entities.fact: The Bahamas are about 700 islands and cays on shallow banks in the Atlantic, where Columbus made his first landfall in 1492.

entities.name: Canary Islands
entities.fact: The Canary Islands are Spanish volcanic islands off north-west Africa, named not after birds but probably after dogs, from the Latin canaria.

entities.name: Greenland
entities.fact: Greenland is the largest island in the world, lying between the Atlantic and Arctic oceans, and about 80 per cent of it is buried under an ice sheet.

entities.name: Cuba
entities.fact: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, sitting where the Atlantic, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea meet.

entities.name: Azores
entities.fact: The Azores are nine volcanic Portuguese islands in the mid-Atlantic, about 1,500 kilometres west of Lisbon, and a famous whale-watching spot.

entities.name: Falkland Islands
entities.fact: The Falkland Islands lie in the South Atlantic about 500 kilometres east of Argentina and have far more sheep and penguins than people.

entities.name: Madeira
entities.fact: Madeira is a Portuguese volcanic island in the Atlantic north of the Canaries, famous for its fortified wine and the laurel forests that once covered it.

entities.name: Cape Verde
entities.fact: Cape Verde is a group of ten volcanic islands off the coast of Senegal, and many Atlantic hurricanes begin as storms passing nearby.

entities.name: Faroe Islands
entities.fact: The Faroe Islands are 18 rugged islands between Norway and Iceland, where sheep outnumber people and the cliffs host huge seabird colonies.

entities.name: Puerto Rico
entities.fact: Puerto Rico lies at the eastern end of the Greater Antilles, and just north of it the Puerto Rico Trench drops to the deepest point in the Atlantic.

entities.name: Great Britain
entities.fact: Great Britain is the largest island in Europe and was joined to the continent by dry land until rising seas flooded Doggerland about 8,000 years ago.

entities.name: Ireland
entities.fact: Ireland is the second-largest island of the British Isles, and the Gulf Stream keeps its climate mild enough for subtropical gardens to thrive on its west coast.

entities.name: Newfoundland
entities.fact: Newfoundland is a large island off eastern Canada where Vikings landed around the year 1000 and whose Grand Banks were once the richest cod fishery on Earth.

entities.name: St Helena
entities.fact: St Helena is a remote volcanic island in the South Atlantic where Napoleon was exiled from 1815 until his death in 1821.

entities.name: Long Island
entities.fact: Long Island stretches about 190 kilometres east from New York City into the Atlantic and is the largest island in the contiguous United States.

entities.name: South Georgia
entities.fact: South Georgia is a mountainous, glacier-covered island in the South Atlantic where Ernest Shackleton is buried and millions of king penguins and fur seals breed.

entities.name: Ascension Island
entities.fact: Ascension Island is a volcanic island in the mid-Atlantic to which green turtles swim about 2,000 kilometres from Brazil to nest on its beaches.

entities.name: Tristan da Cunha
entities.fact: Tristan da Cunha is the most remote inhabited island in the world, with about 250 people living more than 2,000 kilometres from the nearest inhabited land.

entities.name: Shetland
entities.fact: Shetland is the northernmost part of the British Isles, closer to Norway than to Edinburgh, with a long Norse history.

entities.name: Orkney
entities.fact: Orkney, just north of mainland Scotland, is home to Skara Brae, a stone village older than the pyramids, and the natural harbour of Scapa Flow.

entities.name: Hebrides
entities.fact: The Hebrides off Scotland's west coast include Skye, Mull, Lewis and Harris, and the tiny island of Staffa with its basalt Fingal's Cave.

entities.name: Isles of Scilly
entities.fact: The Isles of Scilly lie about 45 kilometres off Cornwall and are warmed by the Gulf Stream so that subtropical plants grow in their gardens.

entities.name: Channel Islands
entities.fact: The Channel Islands of Jersey, Guernsey, Alderney and Sark lie off Normandy and were the only British soil occupied by Germany in the Second World War.

entities.name: Outer Banks
entities.fact: The Outer Banks are a long chain of barrier islands off North Carolina, where the Wright brothers first flew and the pirate Blackbeard was killed.

entities.name: Sable Island
entities.fact: Sable Island is a crescent of sand off Nova Scotia known as the Graveyard of the Atlantic for its hundreds of shipwrecks, and home to wild horses.

entities.name: Fernando de Noronha
entities.fact: Fernando de Noronha is a volcanic archipelago off north-east Brazil famous for its spinner dolphins and strictly limited number of visitors.

entities.name: Bioko
entities.fact: Bioko is a volcanic island in the Gulf of Guinea that holds Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea, far from the country's mainland.

entities.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
entities.fact: São Tomé and Príncipe are two volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea that make up Africa's second-smallest country.

entities.name: Rockall
entities.fact: Rockall is a lone granite rock about 20 metres high in the North Atlantic, west of Scotland, claimed by Britain and argued over for its fishing waters.

entities.name: Surtsey
entities.fact: Surtsey is a volcanic island off Iceland that rose from the sea in 1963 and has been off limits to all but scientists ever since.

entities.name: Skellig Michael
entities.fact: Skellig Michael is a jagged rock off Ireland with a sixth-century monastery on its summit, later used as Luke Skywalker's hideout in Star Wars.

entities.name: Robben Island
entities.fact: Robben Island in Table Bay off Cape Town is where Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for 18 of his 27 years in jail.

entities.name: Bouvet Island
entities.fact: Bouvet Island is the most remote island on Earth, an ice-covered volcanic island in the South Atlantic about 1,700 kilometres from Antarctica with no permanent inhabitants.

entities.name: Alvin
entities.fact: Alvin is the US deep-diving submersible that explored the wreck of the Titanic in 1986 and found the first hydrothermal vent communities in 1977.

entities.name: Calypso
entities.fact: Calypso was a former minesweeper that Jacques Cousteau turned into the floating base for his films and expeditions from 1950 until it sank in Singapore harbour in 1996.

entities.name: Trieste
entities.fact: The bathyscaphe Trieste carried Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 1960, the first crewed dive to the ocean's deepest point.

entities.name: HMS Challenger
entities.fact: HMS Challenger sailed around the world from 1872 to 1876 on the first great oceanographic expedition, sounding the deep that now bears its name.

entities.name: Deepsea Challenger
entities.fact: Deepsea Challenger carried the film director James Cameron alone to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 2012.

entities.name: HMS Beagle
entities.fact: HMS Beagle carried the young Charles Darwin on a five-year surveying voyage around the world from 1831 to 1836 that led to his theory of evolution.

entities.name: Nautilus
entities.fact: The exploration vessel Nautilus, run by Titanic discoverer Robert Ballard's Ocean Exploration Trust, streams its deep-sea dives live to the public.

entities.name: Limiting Factor
entities.fact: Limiting Factor is the submersible in which Victor Vescovo became the first person to dive to the deepest point of all five oceans, in 2018 and 2019.

entities.name: Bathysphere
entities.fact: The bathysphere was a steel ball on a cable in which William Beebe and Otis Barton descended to about 920 metres off Bermuda in 1934, a record that stood for 15 years.

entities.name: Mir
entities.fact: The Russian submersibles Mir-1 and Mir-2 filmed the Titanic wreck for James Cameron's 1997 film and in 2007 planted a flag on the sea floor at the North Pole.

entities.name: Glomar Challenger
entities.fact: The drilling ship Glomar Challenger took cores from the Atlantic floor in 1968 that confirmed sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics.

entities.name: Fram
entities.fact: Fram was built for Fridtjof Nansen to be frozen into the Arctic ice and drift across the polar sea, and later carried Roald Amundsen to Antarctica.

entities.name: RRS Discovery
entities.fact: The Discovery was built for Scott's first Antarctic expedition in 1901, and three later British research ships of the same name have continued its work.

entities.name: Atlantis
entities.fact: Atlantis is the Woods Hole research ship that serves as the mothership for the submersible Alvin.

entities.name: Knorr
entities.fact: The research vessel Knorr was the ship from which Robert Ballard's team found the wreck of the Titanic in 1985.

entities.name: Polarstern
entities.fact: The German icebreaker Polarstern spent a year frozen into Arctic sea ice for the MOSAiC expedition of 2019 to 2020, the largest polar research expedition ever mounted.

entities.name: Shinkai 6500
entities.fact: Japan's Shinkai 6500 can dive to 6,500 metres and was for many years the deepest-diving crewed research submersible in service.

entities.name: Jiaolong
entities.fact: China's submersible Jiaolong dived to more than 7,000 metres in the Mariana Trench in 2012.

entities.name: Kaiko
entities.fact: Kaiko was a Japanese robotic vehicle that in 1995 became the second craft to reach the bottom of the Challenger Deep, and it was lost at sea in 2003.

entities.name: Nereus
entities.fact: Nereus was a hybrid robot submarine that reached the Challenger Deep in 2009 and was lost in the Kermadec Trench in 2014 when it imploded at nearly 10,000 metres.

entities.name: Nautile
entities.fact: Nautile is the French crewed submersible that explored the wreck of the Titanic and recovered thousands of artefacts from it.

entities.name: JOIDES Resolution
entities.fact: The drilling ship JOIDES Resolution spent decades recovering sediment cores from the deep sea floor that record millions of years of Earth's climate.

entities.name: Okeanos Explorer
entities.fact: Okeanos Explorer is a US government ship dedicated entirely to exploring unknown parts of the ocean, broadcasting its dives live online.

entities.name: Falkor
entities.fact: Falkor and its successor Falkor (too) are research ships run by the Schmidt Ocean Institute that offer free ship time to scientists and have mapped vast areas of sea floor.

entities.name: RRS Sir David Attenborough
entities.fact: The polar research ship RRS Sir David Attenborough got its name after a 2016 public vote overwhelmingly chose Boaty McBoatface, a name given to one of its robot submarines instead.

entities.name: Fendouzhe
entities.fact: Fendouzhe, meaning Striver, is the Chinese submersible that carried three people to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 2020.

entities.name: Chikyu
entities.fact: Chikyu is a Japanese drilling ship with a derrick about 120 metres above the water, built to drill deeper into the sea floor than any ship before it.

entities.name: Archimède
entities.fact: The French bathyscaphe Archimède dived to about 9,500 metres in the Kuril Trench in 1962 and later explored the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in Project FAMOUS.

entities.name: Ben Franklin
entities.fact: In 1969 the submersible Ben Franklin drifted silently for 30 days inside the Gulf Stream with six men aboard, a mission NASA studied as a model for long space flights.

entities.name: Albatross
entities.fact: The Albatross, launched in 1882, was the first ship built specifically for marine research and dredged up thousands of new species.

entities.name: Meteor
entities.fact: The German ship Meteor criss-crossed the South Atlantic from 1925 to 1927 using echo sounding to produce the first detailed picture of a whole ocean basin's floor.

entities.name: Galathea
entities.fact: The Danish ship Galathea dredged living animals from more than 10,000 metres in the Philippine Trench in 1951, proving that life exists at the ocean's greatest depths.

entities.name: Akademik Mstislav Keldysh
entities.fact: The Russian research ship Akademik Mstislav Keldysh carries the Mir submersibles and appears as itself in the opening scenes of the film Titanic.

entities.name: Boaty McBoatface
entities.fact: Boaty McBoatface is a yellow robot submarine that won its name in a public vote and has since made long journeys under Antarctic sea ice and deep in the Southern Ocean.

entities.name: Jacques Cousteau
entities.fact: Jacques Cousteau co-invented the Aqua-Lung in 1943, the first successful open-circuit scuba gear, and brought the undersea world to television aboard Calypso.

entities.name: James Cameron
entities.fact: The film director James Cameron made a solo dive to the bottom of the Challenger Deep in 2012 and has visited the Titanic wreck more than 30 times.

entities.name: Robert Ballard
entities.fact: Robert Ballard led the team that found the wreck of the Titanic in 1985 and also located the Bismarck and took part in the discovery of hydrothermal vents.

entities.name: Sylvia Earle
entities.fact: Sylvia Earle, nicknamed Her Deepness, set a record in 1979 by walking the sea floor at 381 metres in a pressurised suit and has spent thousands of hours underwater.

entities.name: Ferdinand Magellan
entities.fact: Ferdinand Magellan led the first expedition to cross the Pacific, which he named for its calm waters, though he was killed in the Philippines before it completed the first circumnavigation.

entities.name: James Cook
entities.fact: Captain James Cook charted more of the Pacific than any navigator before him, crossed the Antarctic Circle, and kept his crews free of scurvy on three great voyages.

entities.name: Jacques Piccard
entities.fact: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960, the first humans ever to do so.

entities.name: Don Walsh
entities.fact: Don Walsh, a US Navy lieutenant, piloted the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of the Challenger Deep with Jacques Piccard in 1960.

entities.name: Victor Vescovo
entities.fact: Victor Vescovo became the first person to reach the deepest point of all five oceans, completing the Five Deeps Expedition in 2019.

entities.name: Christopher Columbus
entities.fact: Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492 on a voyage that opened lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

entities.name: Francis Drake
entities.fact: Sir Francis Drake was the first captain to complete a circumnavigation of the globe, from 1577 to 1580, and the stormy passage below Cape Horn is named after him.

entities.name: William Beebe
entities.fact: William Beebe descended more than 900 metres off Bermuda in the bathysphere in 1934 and was the first scientist to watch deep-sea animals alive in their own world.

entities.name: Auguste Piccard
entities.fact: Auguste Piccard invented the bathyscaphe, a free-diving deep submersible, after first setting altitude records in a stratospheric balloon.

entities.name: Philippe Cousteau
entities.fact: Philippe Cousteau, Jacques Cousteau's younger son, filmed and co-produced many of his father's undersea documentaries before dying in a seaplane crash in 1979.

entities.name: Thor Heyerdahl
entities.fact: Thor Heyerdahl sailed the balsa raft Kon-Tiki about 8,000 kilometres across the Pacific in 1947 to show that ancient people could have made such voyages.

entities.name: Eugenie Clark
entities.fact: Eugenie Clark, the Shark Lady, studied shark behaviour for decades and discovered a Red Sea fish whose secretions repel sharks.

entities.name: Vasco da Gama
entities.fact: Vasco da Gama sailed around the Cape of Good Hope to reach India in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to Asia.

entities.name: Hans Hass
entities.fact: Hans Hass was an Austrian diving pioneer who made some of the first underwater films of sharks and manta rays in the 1940s and 1950s.

entities.name: Jean-Michel Cousteau
entities.fact: Jean-Michel Cousteau, Jacques Cousteau's elder son, founded the Ocean Futures Society and has spent his life making ocean documentaries.

entities.name: Fabien Cousteau
entities.fact: Fabien Cousteau, grandson of Jacques, spent 31 days living in the undersea laboratory Aquarius in 2014, beating his grandfather's record.

entities.name: Rachel Carson
entities.fact: Rachel Carson was a marine biologist whose book The Sea Around Us, published in 1951, introduced millions of readers to the science of the oceans.

entities.name: Jacques Mayol
entities.fact: Jacques Mayol was the free diver who first dived below 100 metres on a single breath in 1976 and inspired the film The Big Blue.

entities.name: Fridtjof Nansen
entities.fact: Fridtjof Nansen let his ship Fram freeze into the Arctic ice to drift across the polar sea and later invented the Nansen bottle for sampling seawater at depth.

entities.name: Zheng He
entities.fact: Zheng He commanded huge Chinese treasure fleets on seven voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433.

entities.name: James Clark Ross
entities.fact: James Clark Ross discovered the Ross Sea and Ross Ice Shelf in 1841 and made some of the first soundings of the deep ocean, reaching below 4,000 metres.

entities.name: Matthew Flinders
entities.fact: Matthew Flinders was the first to sail right around Australia, from 1801 to 1803, and popularised the continent's name.

entities.name: Matthew Fontaine Maury
entities.fact: Matthew Fontaine Maury, known as the Pathfinder of the Seas, compiled ships' logs into the first charts of ocean winds and currents in the 1840s and 1850s.

entities.name: Charles Wyville Thomson
entities.fact: Charles Wyville Thomson was the chief scientist of the Challenger expedition of 1872 to 1876, which laid the foundations of oceanography.

entities.name: Otis Barton
entities.fact: Otis Barton designed and paid for the bathysphere in which he and William Beebe dived in the 1930s, and in 1949 reached about 1,370 metres alone in his benthoscope.

entities.name: Walter Munk
entities.fact: Walter Munk, called the Einstein of the oceans, predicted surf conditions for the D-Day landings and explained how ocean waves travel across whole oceans.

entities.name: Prince Albert I of Monaco
entities.fact: Prince Albert I of Monaco spent his fortune on oceanographic cruises in the 1880s and 1890s and founded the Oceanographic Museum of Monaco.

entities.name: Herbert Nitsch
entities.fact: Herbert Nitsch, the deepest man on Earth, free-dived to 214 metres on a single breath in 2007.

entities.name: Natalia Molchanova
entities.fact: Natalia Molchanova was the most decorated free diver in history, holding dozens of world records, before disappearing on a dive off Ibiza in 2015.

entities.name: Jean-Baptiste Charcot
entities.fact: Jean-Baptiste Charcot led French Antarctic expeditions aboard the ships Français and Pourquoi-Pas? and charted long stretches of the Antarctic Peninsula.

entities.name: Marie Tharp
entities.fact: Marie Tharp drew the first map of the entire ocean floor and spotted the rift valley running down the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, key evidence for continental drift.
